items.title: The science on trans athletes is inconclusive. Cricket’s prejudice isn’t
items.summary: If cricket fans across the eras are to be believed, the game has always been on the brink of extinction. The game should have died yesterday; somehow it survived today, but tomorrow it will definitely slip into oblivion. The unintended consequence of this perpetual mode of apprehension is that on days when there are no real obstacles to overcome and no real issues to solve, imaginary problems must be conjured up, solely because the fight must go on; the chatter machine must keep ticking. Last month, attention fell on women’s cricket, and this purportedly novel effort to ‘save’ it brought in droves of commentators, cricketers, and even those who have always justified its marginal status by claiming it can’t generate more revenue. items.title: The men building AI want us to fear it. We should – but not for the reasons they give
items.summary: Is AI going to run wild and kill us all – or are the concerns lately voiced by the bosses of the AI titans just some kind of convenient business ploy on their part? Those bosses include Dario Amodei of Anthropic, which owns Claude; his rival Sam Altman of OpenAI, which owns ChatGPT and its descendants; and their competitor, SpaceX founder Elon Musk, who owns Grok. The debate has raged around the world for the past few days. Dividing the world into two kinds of people never works, so we’ll go with three: this issue has divided the world into those who agree that AI may indeed kill us all, those who think Musk et al are out to fool us all, and those in the “don’t know/can’t say” camp. Our analysis leads us to think there ought to be a fourth camp: those who agree that the AI bosses may be trying to fool us all, and also that AI may kill us all. The two are not mutually exclusive. Debates over AI safety are old, but the latest drama began with the public resignation of Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher at Anthropic who had earlier worked at OpenAI. items.title: Landslide and flash flood wreak havoc in Kerala: 4 dead, 4 missing
items.summary: Four people died and four others went missing after a landslide and flash flood hit separate locations in Kerala’s Idukki and Malappuram respectively on Sunday, September 20. In Idukki, two people were killed and one person seriously injured when a mudslide swept away a temporary shed at a garlic farm in Kottakkamboor near Munnar’s Vattavada at around 3 pm. The deceased have been identified as Kottakkamboor residents Balakrishnan, 50, and his sister Chinnu, 35. Balakrishnan’s wife Mariyamma, 40, was seriously injured and is undergoing treatment at the Munnar Government Hospital. The three were working at the farm when heavy rain began. They took shelter in a temporary shed, which was struck by the landslide and carried away by the debris. Local residents rescued the three, but Balakrishnan and Chinnu died at the spot. Devikulam Subcollector V M Arya said torrential rain was believed to have triggered the landslide. An electric pole also fell onto the shed during the incident, and authorities are examining whether electrocution contributed to the deaths. items.title: How deficient rainfall is affecting ragi farmers in Karnataka’s Mandya
items.summary: Shiva Shekhar, a 40-year-old farmer from Padavalapatna village in Mandya district's Nagamangala taluk, could not sow ragi this kharif. “I kept waiting for the rain but it never came, so I sowed cowpea instead, which is more drought-tolerant,” he said on September 16. Karnataka is the largest ragi-producing state in the country. In 2025-26, India produced 2 million tonnes of ragi, of which 1.47 million tonnes came from Karnataka, according to the Third Advance Estimates for the year from the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. The state also accounted for about 73% of the area under ragi that year, at 979,000 hectares. Of that, Mandya—located about 40 km north of Mysuru—accounted for about 53,300 hectares. Broadly, ragi sowing at the national and state levels has kept pace with last year. But in Mandya, against a target of 63,385 hectare for this year, ragi was sown in 1,213 hectare (1.91%) by September 11, data shared by Jayaswamy, joint director of agriculture for Mandya, show .
